opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something we ran into very concretely when we started applying Shapley-value-based explanations to things like gene expression data and electronic health records. In biomedical data, features are almost never independent. Genes work in pathways and co-regulated modules, so you'll have dozens or even hundreds of genes whose expression levels move together. In clinical data, things like blood pressure, BMI, age, and various lab values are strongly intertwined.

The issue is that when you compute SHAP values, you need to figure out what happens to the model's prediction when a feature is "missing." The common approach is to simulate that by replacing the feature's value with values drawn from a background distribution, and the simplest and most widely used way of doing that implicitly treats features as independent. When features are highly correlated, that means you end up evaluating the model on combinations of feature values that would never actually occur in reality, say a patient with a particular combination of lab values that's physiologically implausible. The model has never seen data like that, so its behavior there is essentially arbitrary, and the attributions you get can reflect that off-manifold behavior rather than what the model really learned from realistic data.

On the other hand, if you try to respect the correlations and use a conditional approach, you run into a different conceptual issue. Credit gets spread across correlated features, so a feature the model doesn't even use can receive importance just because it's correlated with one that it does use. Whether that's desirable depends on the question you're asking. Are you trying to understand the model, or are you trying to understand the underlying biology? Those are different goals, and people often conflate them.

There's also a practical consequence for discovery. If a hundred genes are all capturing the same biological signal, the attribution can get diluted across all of them, so no single gene looks very important, even though the underlying pathway is strongly predictive. Or, depending on the model, one gene might arbitrarily get all the credit while its equally relevant neighbors get none. If a biologist then takes the top-ranked genes and goes into the lab to validate them, that instability really matters, because it affects which hypotheses get pursued.

So a lot of our work has focused on that: being explicit about which kind of question you're answering, and developing approaches that account for correlation structure, for example by attributing to groups of features or by ensembling over models so that the explanations are more robust and more biologically meaningful. In biomedicine, explanations aren't just a nice add-on. They're often the actual scientific output, so getting this right is really important.

r001.rationale: The response says attribution can be diluted across correlated genes or assigned arbitrarily to one gene, but it does not state that perfectly correlated genes admit infinitely many possible allocations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. So the issue really comes down to what SHAP is actually trying to do. SHAP values are grounded in Shapley values from cooperative game theory, and the way you compute them is by asking, for every feature, what happens to the model's prediction when that feature is present versus when it's absent. And "absent" is the tricky part, because a trained model doesn't know how to make a prediction with a feature missing. So you have to simulate absence somehow, and the common way to do that is to replace the missing feature with values drawn from some background distribution, often treating features as if they were independent of each other.

Now in biomedical data, that independence assumption is almost never true. Think about gene expression data. You might have thousands of genes, and many of them are co-regulated, they sit in the same pathway, they move together. Or in clinical data, you have things like systolic and diastolic blood pressure, or creatinine and BUN, which are strongly correlated because they're reflecting the same underlying physiology. When you perturb one of those features independently, you're creating input combinations that never occur in reality, say, a patient with very high systolic pressure and very low diastolic pressure. The model has never seen anything like that, and so the output it gives you in that region is essentially extrapolation. It's not meaningful, but SHAP will still happily attribute credit based on it.

So that's one problem, the attributions can be built on off-manifold evaluations of the model. The second problem is more conceptual. When two features carry essentially the same information, there's a real ambiguity about who should get the credit. The Shapley axioms will split it in some principled way, but the split depends on what the model happened to learn. If a tree-based model latched onto gene A rather than gene B, SHAP will tell you gene A is important and gene B isn't, even though biologically they may be interchangeable. And that's dangerous when a clinician or a biologist is looking at these explanations trying to generate hypotheses, because they might conclude gene B doesn't matter when really it just lost a coin flip during training.

And then there's the flip side, which is that if you try to respect the correlation structure, say by conditioning on the observed features when you sample the missing ones, you end up spreading importance across correlated features, and now features that the model doesn't actually use can get nonzero attribution. So neither choice is obviously right. It depends on whether your question is "what is this model using" or "what in the data is actually associated with the outcome." Those are different questions, and in biomedicine people often conflate them.

So a lot of our work has been about being explicit about that distinction, and about developing methods that either model the dependencies more faithfully or at least make clear what assumptions the explanation is resting on. Because ultimately the goal in these settings isn't just a pretty bar chart, it's to generate scientific insight or support a clinical decision, and if the explanation is an artifact of an independence assumption that doesn't hold, you can be very confidently wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes ambiguity in assigning credit to genes that carry essentially the same information, but it does not state that perfectly correlated genes allow infinitely many possible attribution allocations.

astra-6.text:
In biomedical data, features are often highly correlated. You may have many genes participating in the same pathway, so their expression levels move together. A model might use one of those genes, but another gene could provide almost the same predictive information. That makes it difficult to interpret an attribution as saying, “This particular gene is uniquely important.”

For SHAP, the key question is how we represent a feature being missing. If we sample features independently, we can break those correlations and evaluate the model on combinations that are biologically unrealistic. If we preserve the correlations by conditioning on the observed features, a feature can receive attribution because it carries information about another feature—even if the model doesn’t directly use it.

So the challenge is deciding which question we want the explanation to answer. Are we explaining what the model uses, or how much information a feature provides given the relationships in the data? Neither of those, by itself, tells us that a gene causes a disease. That distinction is especially important when we use explanations to generate biological hypotheses.

r001.rationale: The response says correlated genes can carry nearly the same predictive information, making unique importance difficult to interpret. It does not state that perfectly correlated genes allow infinitely many ways to allocate attribution between them.

sol-6.1.text:
In biomedical data, features are often highly correlated. Multiple genes may participate in the same pathway, for example, so their expression levels move together. A model can use one gene as a substitute for another, which makes it difficult to assign credit to individual features.

For SHAP, an important question is what we mean by a feature being “missing.” If we sample it independently of the other features, we can create combinations that are biologically unrealistic. If we preserve the correlations, a feature can receive credit because it provides information about another feature the model actually uses. Those approaches answer different questions.

So the challenge is interpreting the attribution correctly. A large SHAP value tells us something about a model’s prediction under particular assumptions; it does not, by itself, establish that a gene causes the biological outcome.

r001.rationale: The response explains that correlated genes make individual credit difficult to assign, but it does not state that perfectly correlated genes admit infinitely many possible attribution allocations.
